rows: 40 places · the signature of Ho Chi Minh City

rows.w: The 'Commando Cafe' - a 1940s house that was a secret Viet Cong special-forces base with a weapons bunker and hidden mailbox; today it pours nostalgic bac xiu and serves com tam Dai Han above its wartime tunnel.
North-to-South phở institution since 1954, famed for its giant 'to xe lua' (train-car) bowl of simple, garnish-free Northern phở bac that Saigonese have loved for 70+ years.
A perennially packed bún bò Huế spot beside the Conservatory of Music, singled out by a visiting New York chef as one of the best bowls of soup in all of Vietnam.
Beloved home-cooking restaurant in restored villas; MICHELIN Bib Gourmand, rice cooked in cast iron on wood stoves.
Nguyen Thi Thanh's canalside stall made famous by Bourdain's No Reservations; a different regional noodle soup each day.

A 300m alley market settled by Vietnamese-Cambodian refugees in the 1970s, now Saigon's densest Cambodian-Vietnamese food alley (100+ stalls); Khmer fish noodles, prahok and palm-sugar chè, from ~3pm.
Saigon's most famous banh mi since 1989 — permanent queues for the thap cam loaded with pate and cold cuts.
Chef Peter Cuong Franklin's MICHELIN-starred restaurant over the Ton That Dam market; street food reimagined as fine dining.
One of Saigon's oldest phở houses, founded 1947 by Mr Tran Van Phon and still simmering its crystal-clear, lightly sweet broth over a charcoal stove; now second/third generation.
Canalside beef pho stall; MICHELIN Bib Gourmand 2024-2026, famed for its long-braised oxtail.
Alley pho institution serving Saigonese since 1945; MICHELIN Bib Gourmand, pairs its broth with pate chaud.
Nearly-century-old banh mi cart (est. 1930), now third generation, with homemade pate and pork roll.

rows: 58 places · the top tier, graded within each area

rows.w: The twin-spired red-brick French cathedral (1863-1880) built with imported Marseille materials, on the square opposite the Post Office. UNDER RESTORATION since 2017 (interior closed to visitors; completion pushed to ~2027, scaffolding coming off by early 2026) — view the exterior.

The 'Commando Cafe' - a 1940s house that was a secret Viet Cong special-forces base with a weapons bunker and hidden mailbox; today it pours nostalgic bac xiu and serves com tam Dai Han above its wartime tunnel.

rows.n: Sủi Cảo Hà Tôn Quyền (Thiên Thiên)
rows.w: The heart of Saigon's nicknamed 'phố sủi cảo' — a cluster of Hoa family dumpling shops (Thiên Thiên among the best-known) that have run for 30+ years each. Plump shrimp-and-pork sủi cảo steamed, fried, or in clear soup with handmade noodles.

The modernist 1960s presidential palace where NVA Tank 843 crashed the gate on 30 April 1975, ending the war. Frozen-in-time state rooms, war-command bunker and telecoms basement. National monument; daily ~07:00-18:00, 80,000d.

Working 1886-1891 post office (architect Alfred Foulhoux; often mis-credited to Eiffel) with a vaulted iron-truss hall, painted maps and a portrait of Ho Chi Minh. Ranked among the world's most beautiful post offices; still operational.

Saigon's most atmospheric Taoist temple, built by the Cantonese community in 1909, thick with incense smoke and carved wooden deities incl. the Hall of Ten Hells and a turtle pond. Obama visited in 2016. Free, ~07:00-18:00.

rows.n: Nguyen Hue Walking Street & People's Committee Building
rows.w: The city's 900 m pedestrian boulevard (a former canal, walkerised 2015) running from the floodlit French Hotel de Ville / People's Committee Building (1898-1909, viewed from outside) and Ho Chi Minh statue down to the Saigon River. Liveliest at night.

Saigon's only Hindu temple, a vivid South-Indian shrine built by Tamil merchants in the late 1800s to the goddess Mariamman, its ~12 m gopuram crowded with painted deities. Free; daily ~07:00-19:00, remove shoes.

The 1.3 km riverside park and pier on the Saigon River where locals gather at sunset and river cruises and the 15,000d public waterbus depart for Thu Duc. The best way to see the city from the water, past Landmark 81 and Bitexco.

The city's newest icon — a cable-stayed bridge with a single soaring pylon, opened April 2022, linking central District 1 (Mê Linh Square) to the Thủ Thiêm new-urban area. Its artistic night lighting and the riverside park beneath it have made it one of Saigon's most popular sunset and check-in spots on the water.

rows.n: Tuyến Metro số 1 Bến Thành - Suối Tiên (Metro Line 1)
rows.w: The city's first metro, opened 22 December 2024 after more than a decade of building — and an instant 'triệu-like' check-in phenomenon in its own right. The Bến Thành underground hall's lotus-shaped skylight and the elevated An Phú and Thảo Điền stations (sunset views over Thủ Đức) are the most-photographed spots; ride it as an attraction, not just transport.
North-to-South phở institution since 1954, famed for its giant 'to xe lua' (train-car) bowl of simple, garnish-free Northern phở bac that Saigonese have loved for 70+ years.

An early-19th-century pagoda built on the foundations of an ancient Khmer/Oc Eo-era temple mound, a recognised National Historical-Cultural Monument with a fine timber-framed Southern-style hall. A quiet, deeply historic stop in District 11.

The city's main venue for mua roi nuoc (water puppetry), the thousand-year-old northern folk art performed on a pool of water with live traditional musicians. Two short shows daily (17:00 and 18:30) beside Tao Dan Park.

The city's oldest hotel (1880) on former Rue Catinat opposite the Opera House, where Graham Greene wrote much of 'The Quiet American' in Room 214 and its terrace was the correspondents' 1950s watering hole. A living piece of literary and war-era Saigon.

The 262 m lotus-bud tower (2010) with a helipad wing and the 49th-floor Saigon Skydeck, the city's first observation deck, giving 360-degree views over the river. Open daily ~09:30-21:30.

A crumbling 1960s nine-storey block (once housing for US advisers) reborn as a vertical warren of independent cafes, boutiques and bars, each balcony overlooking the walking street. Slow lift ~3,000d, or take the stairs.

The open-air rooftop bar of the 1960 Rex Hotel, site of the US military's daily wartime press briefings mocked as the 'Five O'Clock Follies'. Iconic Vietnam-War history plus sweeping views over Nguyen Hue and City Hall.

A 50-hectare cultural-and-amusement park in District 11 with landscaped gardens, thrill rides, cultural exhibits and an adjoining water park. One of the city's big family day-outs, alongside Suoi Tien and Dai Nam.

rows.n: Đền thờ Vua Hùng (Hung Kings Temple, Thao Cam Vien)
rows.w: A near-century-old temple inside the Botanical Gardens, built by the French in 1926 as a 'Temple du souvenir' and rededicated after 1954 to the Hùng Kings and other national heroes. Modeled on Huế imperial-palace architecture with a 3-ton bronze elephant in the forecourt; the focal point of Saigon's Giỗ Tổ Hùng Vương observances each third lunar month.

rows.n: Kênh Nhiêu Lộc - Thị Nghè (Nhieu Loc Canal)
rows.w: A nearly 10 km 'green ribbon' through the inner city — once a dead, polluted canal, reborn after a decade-long clean-up into landscaped embankments and a signature of Saigon's revival. Since 2015 a 4.5 km guided boat tour (covered wooden boats and hand-rowed phụng boats) runs it with đờn ca tài tử music; the multi-coloured bridge lighting is a night check-in.

A shaded central park laid out in 1983 over the former Massiges (European) Cemetery, once the resting place of colonial elites and President Ngo Dinh Diem. A leafy escape with a fascinating buried history documented by Saigoneer.

rows.n: Công viên Lê Thị Riêng (Le Thi Rieng Park)
rows.w: A green, lake-dotted culture park on Cách Mạng Tháng Tám — built in 1983 on the cleared Chí Hòa cemetery — that doubles as a family playground with the 'Thỏ Trắng' rides, pool, weekend magic shows and street-food stalls. Free entry; a local weekend hangout rather than a headline sight.
